items.title: Headlines for October 27, 2026 | Democracy Now!
items.excerpt: ## Netanyahu Battles to Hold Power as Israel Holds First Election in Four Years Oct 27, 2026 Voters in Israel are heading to the polls today in the first general election in nearly four years. At stake are 120 seats in Israel’s parliament, the Knesset, where 61 votes will be needed to form a majority. Likud party leader Benjamin Netanyahu is seeking to extend his term as Israel’s longest-serving prime minister — that’s despite a warrant issued by the International Criminal Court seeking his arrest for war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Gaza. Netanyahu also faces criminal charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust. His main challenger is Israel’s former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, who supports illegal Israeli settlements, opposes a Palestinian state and has vowed to destroy Hamas’s military wing in Gaza within 18 months. A prominent Palestinian citizen of Israel, Sami Abu Shehadeh, who leads the Palestinian nationalist political party Balad, was forced out of the race. Meanwhile, millions of Palestinians living under Israeli occupation in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza Strip are ineligible to vote — even as election officials set up polling stations in illegal Israeli settlements. ## U.N. Commission of Inquiry Finds Israel Committed Genocide in Gaza, War Crimes in West Bank Oct 27, 2026 A United Nations commission of inquiry has accused Israel of committing genocide in the Gaza Strip during the war that followed the October 7, 2023, attacks. The report published Monday by the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory found Israel’s attacks on Gaza were intended to “destroy the Palestinian people, in whole or in part.” The commission also accused Israel of committing crimes against humanity in the occupied West Bank, including extermination, torture and rape. The report was released as Israeli attacks on Gaza killed at least five Palestinians, including a 7-year-old girl. Meanwhile, in the occupied West Bank, Israeli forces have continued a large-scale offensive for a fifth consecutive day in the city of Hebron, where officials say nearly 5,000 Palestinians have been forced from their homes. ## Humanitarian Crisis Grows as Houthis Lay Siege to Yemen’s Third-Largest City Oct 27, 2026 In Yemen, Ansar Allah, known as the Houthis, used explosives to severely damage a critical road into Taiz, according to Human Rights Watch. The Hayjat al-Abd road is critical for delivering food, medicine and fuel to the city. Taiz has been besieged since fighting escalated between the Saudi-backed government and Ansar Allah. Fuel shortages in Taiz are straining hospitals, with one hospital forced to cut the number of ​incubators, putting newborn babies at risk. This is a neonatal nurse at the Yemeni-Swedish Hospital. > Nada Ahmed: “We reduced the numbers to 10 incubators because of the fuel shortage. There’s no oxygen. There’s no fuel to run the incubators, to keep the babies warm. We also moved from upstairs to downstairs for the babies’ safety. There is shelling near the hospital.” ## Seven Are Killed as Jordan Bombs Syria Following Deadly Church Attack Oct 27, 2026 In Syria, officials say seven people were killed, including women, children and an elderly man, after Jordan’s military struck sites in Daraa and Suwayda provinces. Jordan’s military said its fighter jets had killed and wounded “several terrorists,” without elaborating. The strikes followed a shooting at a Greek Orthodox church in Jordan on Friday that left nine people dead and 34 injured. Earlier on Monday, Jordan’s government said it had arrested three suspects behind the deadly church ​attack. ## Health Worker Killed in DRC as Ebola Cases Approach 10,000 Oct 27, 2026 In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, youths wielding machetes attacked two community health workers who were raising awareness of the Ebola outbreak in the country, killing one and wounding another. A local official said health workers in the area where the latest attack took place are sheltering at ​the general hospital under ⁠police guard. This is a U.N. spokesperson on the latest. > Daniela Gross de Almeida: “These incidents highlight how violence and mistrust can undermine the Ebola response and limit access to essential health services, as the numbers of confirmed cases approach 10,000, according to national authorities.” ## Russia and Ukraine Trade Drone Attacks Despite Local Ceasefire in Russian-Occupied Oleshky Oct 27, 2026 In Ukraine, a local ceasefire is underway in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, where fighting has left residents cut off from food and medical aid. The rare ceasefire to allow humanitarian access was brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump. Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine continue to trade attacks elsewhere. Overnight, Russia launched hundreds of drones and ballistic missiles across Ukraine, killing at least one person and injuring 15 others in the capital Kyiv, including students in a dormitory. And Russian officials said a Ukrainian drone killed a man and wounded six people in the western Russian city of Bryansk near Ukraine’s border, while another person was killed and 30 injured when a drone hit a bus in Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia. Meanwhile, a new report submitted to the U.N. General Assembly finds Russian officials committed war crimes by directing attacks against civilian targets in Ukraine, as well as crimes against humanity through continuous attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. This is Pablo de Greiff, a member of the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine. > Pablo de Greiff: “Those attacks that target civilian objects indispensable to the civilian population are unlawful and amount to war crimes.” In Brazil, far-right presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro has backed off his pledge to challenge the results of Sunday’s election, after results showed incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won by nearly 4.5 million votes. Bolsonaro’s concession came just minutes after President Trump signaled he would not intervene on Bolsonaro’s behalf — although Trump did state, without evidence, that the vote “looked like another rigged election.” Bolsonaro also said Brazil’s Supreme Court had ordered police to seize his passport. According to The New York Times, Bolsonaro faces a criminal investigation over his links to a Brazilian lawyer accused of laundering more than $1 billion through a fraud scheme.

items.title: Q3 earnings show resilient U.S. consumer, signs of strain
items.excerpt: Published Tue, Oct 27 2026 2:00 PM EDT Updated 2 Hours Ago ... One word keeps appearing in third-quarter earnings reports: "resilient." That's the early read on U.S. consumers from various companies that released their results this week. Many businesses say Americans are still spending despite inflationary pressures, though not every company has enjoyed the same success. The commentary comes amid fears that diesel fuel prices, which hit an all-time high of $6.52 per gallon in September, would drive up prices on consumer products. Economists also worried that more expensive regular gas, combined with high borrowing costs and continued tension between the U.S. and Iran, would spur a pullback in consumer spending. Retail sales rose 0.8% in September, following a jump of 1.3% in August. Sales in September were boosted by rising gas station spending. Despite all those challenges, some corporate executives say the headwinds aren't yet affecting sales.

items.title: Economy, the Fed, and Rates…
items.excerpt: October 27, 2026 Economic Data & Labor Market - Higher rates are weighing on housing. Pending home sales fell 7.3% in September to an index level of 66.0, the lowest in National Association of Realtors data back to 2001, and housing starts dropped 5.2% to a 1.221 million annual rate, a four-month low. NAHB builder sentiment fell to 29 on October 19, the lowest since June 2012. Freddie Mac’s 30-year rate eased to 7.32% on October 22 from 7.40%, versus 6.19% a year earlier, but MBA purchase applications fell 7% in the week ended October 16 and were 18% below a year earlier. In the University of Michigan’s final October survey, 85% of consumers called it a bad time to buy a home, the largest share in more than two years. - Business activity remains strong and price pressures persist. S&P Global’s flash October composite PMI registered 57.6, with the manufacturing PMI at 56.0, a 53-month high. New orders across manufacturing and services grew at the fastest pace in more than four years. Businesses reported raising the prices they charge customers at the fastest pace since August 2022, citing higher oil and freight costs and tariffs. Initial claims fell 6,000 to 194,000 for the week ended October 17 from an upwardly revised 200,000, while continuing claims rose to 1.728 million for the week ended October 10, a six-week high. Michigan’s survey showed consumers’ year-ahead inflation expectations rising to 4.7%. - The October 27–29 calendar brings growth and inflation into focus. Durable goods and new home sales arrive Tuesday, October 27. The advance GDP estimate and September PCE inflation data follow on Thursday, October 29, with the Bloomberg median at 3.2% annualized GDP growth versus 2.2% in the second quarter. Federal Reserve Policy - An October hold is expected, with a rate hike favored by December. With the federal funds target at 3.75%–4.00% and officials in the pre-meeting blackout, Bloomberg’s futures-based pricing showed investors strongly favored an October hold but priced in most of a quarter-point rate increase by the December 9 meeting. - The data cut both ways for the Committee. On one side are the PMI price indices, inflation expectations, and September CPI inflation at 3.7% year over year; on the other are a housing market weakened by high mortgage rates, an equity market questioning AI capital spending, and global corporate bond spreads at a 17-month high. The Financial Times interpreted the Treasury rally as investors seeking safety in government bonds, with little change in bond-market inflation expectations. As oil prices surged on October 23, however, a bond-market measure of expected annual inflation over the next five years rose from 2.39% to 2.47%.

items.title: U.S. Treasury yields: Federal Reserve's monetary policy meeting begins
items.excerpt: Treasury yields moved higher on Tuesday as the Federal Reserve's two-day monetary policy meeting kicked off and investors digested a spate of economic data releases. The benchmark 10-year Treasury Add To Watchlist yield rose less than 1 basis point to 4.995%, as did the 30-year Treasury Add To Watchlist bond to 5.309%. The 2-year Treasury Add To Watchlist note yield was up more than 2 basis points at 4.737%. One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions. The Fed is scheduled to announce its monetary policy decision on Wednesday at the conclusion of its meeting. Traders are widely expecting policymakers to keep the interest rate unchanged at the current target range of 3.75% to 4%, but will look for clues as to whether the Fed will hike interest rates again before the end of the year. Fed funds futures trading is now pricing in a nearly 93% chance that the Fed will hold rates steady, according to the CME FedWatch Tool. ... Those on Wall Street on Tuesday assessed the latest reading on durable goods orders, which increased 1.8% in September. That was slightly above the 1.7% rise that economists polled by Dow Jones expected. ... In September, new home sales stood at 676,000, marking a 0.6% fall from August but coming in above the 653,000 Dow Jones consensus estimate. Meanwhile, consumer confidence in October rose to 91.7, beating the 81.0 that was estimated.

items.title: New poll shows Democrats have midterm edge ...
items.excerpt: Democrats retain significant midterm electoral advantages, with key data pointing to them being the favorites to win control of the U.S. House. But, there are indications of why a potential wave could be limited, a new NPR/PBS News/Marist poll finds. The poll also sheds light on the issues driving voters across the ideological spectrum. The cost of living continues to be top of mind overall with a third of people saying they've experienced financial hardship in the past year and 4 in 10 saying their personal finances have gotten worse. "The economy is at the top of my list right now," said Shun Maurice, a 47-year-old from Arizona who participated in the poll. He's an independent who leans toward Democrats and said high food and gas prices are a strain. "They're too expensive for everybody, no matter who you voted for," he said. "They're just too expensive for the American people in general, and I don't like that." Preserving democracy also continues to resonate with Democrats and independents, while immigration is the biggest concern for self-described MAGA supporters. The poll of 1,289 registered voters was conducted Oct. 19-20. When registered voters are mentioned, the margin of error is +/- 3.7 percentage points. When likely voters are mentioned, it is +/- 3.8 points. ### Most don't think Trump is doing a good job and don't like him This was the first survey this cycle that Marist applied a likely voter screen, and on multiple questions, likely voters were — within the margin of error — slightly less likely than registered voters to disapprove of the president. Likely voters overall were also slightly less likely to want Democrats to run Congress. Likely voters are something of a special sauce in polling. Survey researchers apply various metrics — like levels of enthusiasm, past voting history and how important voting is to different respondents — to try to identify the subsample of people who are most likely to vote. In this survey, just 38% of registered voters approved of the job President Trump is doing, with 61% disapproving (-23). Likely voters gave him a 40% to 59% rating (-19), still not very good, but even a slight margin can make a difference in how significant the gains either party might make in the election are. That said, an equal share — 53% — of registered and likely voters said they "strongly disapprove" of the job Trump is doing, tied with last month as the highest ever in the poll. Trump's favorability rating is even lower — just 37% of likely voters have a favorable impression of Trump, while 59% have a negative one. ### Democrats retain the edge on the congressional ballot Democrats also had a strong advantage on which party's candidate people said they are more likely to vote for in their district if the election were held today, known as the generic congressional ballot. Among registered voters, it was a 10-point advantage. With likely voters, it was 8 points, still indicative of Democratic gains. When Democrats have had that kind of lead on the congressional ballot, they have historically done very well. On average, it was +7 in 2018 and +12 in 2006. In both years, Democrats won the House with at least 30 seats flipped. But that was before the 2020 Census and ensuing regular redistricting — and the rare, mid-decade redistricting in the last year and a half after Trump asked Republican states to redraw their maps to potentially give Republicans more seats. Though Democrats followed suit, both redistricting periods have tilted congressional seats in Republicans' direction and given them a relative advantage nationally. Perhaps because of some of those structural disadvantages and past performance, there is a notable degree of nervousness among Democrats. While 98% of Democratic likely voters said they would vote for a Democrat, just 81% thought the Democrat would win, a 17-point difference. Republicans were only 10 points less likely to believe their candidate would win. Notably, among independents, a higher share thought the Democratic candidate would win. ... ### Democrats also have the enthusiasm advantage, but there are some caution flags, too Democratic likely voters are 10 points more likely to say they are "very enthusiastic" about voting (71% vs. 61%). That's actually wider than the difference between Democratic and Republican registered voters in the poll. The caution for Democrats, though, is that several of their key pillar groups are not very enthusiastic to vote, and Republicans have closed the gap on who is following the election "very closely." Just 42% of likely voters under 45, 53% of non-white voters and 56% of white women with college degrees said they are "very enthusiastic" to vote. All of those groups disapproved of the job Trump is doing. Compare that to pro-Trump groups — MAGA voters (68%), white women without degrees (66%) and white evangelical voters (61%). For independents, 48% report being very enthusiastic to vote. Traditionally, younger, as well as Black and Latino voters turn out at disproportionately lower rates in midterm elections. But with the realignment under Trump, more white, college-educated voters are voting Democratic and, as a group, they turn out at the highest rates. When it comes to paying close attention, last month just 34% of registered Republicans said they're following the election very closely, compared to 42% of Democrats. Now, they're even – 46% of Democrats and 45% of Republicans said they're paying very close attention. When it comes to likely voters, there's no difference either – 51% of Democrats to 50% of Republicans. On the positive side for Democrats: those who voted for Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024 are 15 points more likely than Trump 2024 voters to say they are very enthusiastic. And Democrats overall have an 8-point advantage over Republicans when it comes to who cares a "great deal" about who controls Congress. ... Three-quarters of likely voters are confident that their state and local governments will run a fair and accurate election. That includes solid majorities of Democrats (88%), Republicans (68%) and independents (75%), but Republicans were 20 points less likely than Democrats to think they would be run well. MAGA supporters were almost 30 points less likely.

items.excerpt: # AP Entertainment SummaryBrief at 9:37 a.m. EDT - AP - Oct 27, 2026 - Oct 27, 2026 Updated 39 mins ago Taylor Swift, Lyle Lovett and more inducted into Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Taylor Swift has been inducted into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame, alongside Lyle Lovett, Shawn Camp, Lee Thomas Miller, Bruce Channel and J.I. Allison. Swift signed her first publishing deal in Nashville at the age of 14. She returned to the city on Monday during the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame annual gala celebration. She said it was an incredible honor to be inducted and described soaking up the lessons from other writers like a sponge. Also honored was country music icon George Strait with the organization's Career Maker Award. He said the songwriters helped to make his career. Jay-Z picks himself to headline the Super Bowl halftime show at SoFi Stadium in Southern California LOS ANGELES (AP) — Jay-Z will headline the Super Bowl halftime show on February 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California. The NFL, Apple Music, and Roc Nation announced the news Monday night. NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said he always wanted Jay-Z to perform when the time felt right. Jay-Z expressed excitement about the opportunity, calling it a dream come true. His Roc Nation has partnered with the NFL since 2019 to produce entertainment presentations, including the halftime show. Jay-Z, who has won 25 Grammy Awards, will perform at the stadium where he recently celebrated the 30th anniversary of his debut album, “Reasonable Doubt.” Andrea Bocelli concerts in Indonesia to proceed despite opposition from Muslim clerics JAKARTA, Indonesia (AP) — Italian tenor Andrea Bocelli's concerts in Indonesia will proceed despite opposition from the country's top Muslim clerical body. The Indonesian Ulema Council demanded the cancellation due to Bocelli's past support for Israel. Indonesia, a strong supporter of Palestinians, does not have formal diplomatic relations with Israel. The concerts are scheduled for October 31 at Borobudur Temple and November 3 in Jakarta. Promoter Shoemaker Live insists the events will support Indonesia's tourism and culture sectors. Bocelli plans to dedicate songs to humanity and world peace. The council argues the concerts could hurt Indonesians who support Palestinians. After pushback, the Dutch reverse course and withdraw from Eurovision again AMSTERDAM (AP) — The Netherlands is withdrawing from participating in the Eurovision Song Contest, reversing a decision in September to return to the show. NPO, the umbrella organization for public broadcasters in the country announced in September it would send a performer to the event, after a subsidiary had said a month earlier it would boycott the contest for a second year. Earlier this month, hundreds of NPO employees sent a letter opposing Dutch participation. A number of prominent Dutch media personalities also publicly objected to the move. Japanese manga artist Tetsuya Chiba, known for his boxing masterpiece 'Ashita no Joe,' dies at 87 TOKYO (AP) — Tetsuya Chiba, a legendary Japanese manga artist best known for his boxing series “Ashita no Joe,” or “Fighting for Tomorrow,” has died. He was 87. Chiba’s masterpiece “Ashita no Joe” series, depicting an aspiring young generation during Japan’s postwar era, became a national sensation. The series was so popular that fans even attended a mock funeral for the protagonist’s rival. Chiba was also a vocal supporter of peace and freedom of expression, telling stories of his harrowing memories of war as a child in his autobiographical stories and manga. Chiba’s publisher, Kodansha Ltd., said Tuesday that the artist died at a Tokyo hospital last Thursday. Music Review: Nickelback is in familiar form on cameo-heavy 'Everything Under the Sun' Nickelback’s 11th studio album “Everything Under the Sun” is a mix of hard-rock anthems, radio-friendly hits, and emotional ballads with a few surprises. The Canadian rockers mostly stick to their successful formula, which has been both criticized and celebrated for over 30 years. The Associated Press' Dennis Waszak Jr. says in his review that the album out Friday is a showcase of everything Nickelback does best. Highlights on the 12-track album include the high-energy “Rattle The Cage” and rock ballads “I Already Know” and “Make Me Love You.” Guest appearances include Sammy Hagar and actor Ryan Reynolds. But those looking for more than their formula may not enjoy it. Walter Koenig, Ensign Chekov on the original 'Star Trek' series, dies at 90 LOS ANGELES (AP) — Actor Walter Koenig, known for playing Ensign Pavel Chekov on “Star Trek,” has died at 90. His talent agent confirmed he passed away Monday at his home in Los Angeles. Koenig's role as Chekov showcased a future where rival nations worked together. “Star Trek” aired from 1966 to 1969 and gained a massive fan following. Koenig's castmate George Takei praised him as a writer, teacher, and friend. Koenig appeared in seven “Star Trek” movies and wrote a book about the series. He also acted in “Babylon 5” and ventured into computer games. Pioneering industrial band Ministry is done. Take it from founder Al Jourgensen: 'It's time to go' NEW YORK (AP) — Ministry, the pioneering industrial rock band that paved the way for acts like Nine Inch Nails, is calling it quits after 45 years. Founder Al Jourgensen confirms the band is done after releasing their 17th album, “Hate To Go — Take Out Or Delivery,” on Oct. 30. A farewell tour will follow. Jourgensen told The Associated Press he believes it's time for a new generation to take over. The final album reflects their multidecade run without leaning into nostalgia and utilizes artificial intelligence in unsettling and surprising ways. Jourgensen jokes about retiring to herd goats and denies wanting a lasting legacy. “We did what we could,” he says of his band. Chris Brown avoids prison time for brawling at a London nightclub LONDON (AP) — Chris Brown has avoided prison time for beating a music producer with a tequila bottle at a London nightclub three years ago. On Monday, a court gave him an eight-month sentence, suspended for a year. Brown, 37, faced up to three years in prison after pleading guilty to affray in July. The incident occurred at Tape, a private club in Mayfair, in February 2023. Affray involves unlawful violence that causes fear for safety. Brown's plea deal led prosecutors to drop more serious charges. He was arrested in May 2025 after returning to the UK for a concert. What to Stream: 'Minions & Monsters,' Matthew Perry, Daddy Yankee and 'The Gilded Age' A new docuseries about Matthew Perry and the latest Minions movie are among the new streaming releases this week. The Minions return in “Minions & Monsters,” where they become silent movie stars in the 1920s. On Paramount+, “Hanging by a Wire” chronicles a dramatic 2023 rescue in Pakistan. Daddy Yankee releases a new album, “La Postal,” exploring themes of love. Nickelback and Dustin Lynch also have new albums out. On Netflix, a docuseries on Matthew Perry premieres Tuesday. “The Gilded Age” returns for its fourth season on HBO Max. Plus, the video game “Phantom Blade Zero” debuts Thursday.
